title: Puliša’s ritual

dating.label: attested 14th–13th c. BCE
dating.note: The surviving copies are in New Hittite script. This is an approximate manuscript date, not a year assigned to the ritual’s composition.

purpose: A ritual for plague brought home after a campaign: people and animals stand in for the king and carry the affliction back toward enemy territory.

phases.name: Human substitutes
phases.idea: A man and woman receive garments and spoken appeals.

phases.name: Animal substitutes
phases.idea: Bull and ewe are brought forward; wool and words transfer the plague.

phases.name: Dispatch
phases.idea: The animals move ahead of the human substitutes.

steps.title: Select a prisoner and a woman
steps.shortDescription: A prisoner of war and a woman from the enemy land are chosen as substitutes.
steps.summary: A prisoner of war and a woman from the enemy land are chosen as substitutes.
steps.patient: One prisoner of war and one woman
steps.evidence: The action is described in obv. I 6–7.

image.alt: The two people are shown neutrally; their physical appearance and clothing are not described.
image.note: The two people are shown neutrally; their physical appearance and clothing are not described.

steps.title: Address the male deity
steps.shortDescription: The speaker offers the adorned man as a substitute and asks that he carry the plague away.
steps.summary: The speaker offers the adorned man as a substitute and asks that he carry the plague away.
steps.recipient: A male deity of the enemy land

image.alt: The male and female human substitutes in festive clothing.
image.note: The pair represents the chosen substitutes; the utterance itself has no recoverable visual form.

steps.title: Address the female deity
steps.shortDescription: The corresponding words are spoken to the woman concerning a female deity.
steps.summary: The corresponding words are spoken to the woman concerning a female deity.
steps.recipient: A female deity of the enemy land

image.alt: Festive garments for the female substitute.
image.note: The plain dress refers to the female substitute; the preserved text says the words were repeated for a female deity.
